intro: Artur Schnabel plays the fierce E-minor middle movement of Op. 109. Running quavers give way to whispered exchanges between the hands before the opening bursts back.

sections.label: A · E minor, then B minor
sections.mNote: A running melody above a strongly marked bass

sections.label: Dev · The bass becomes the tune
sections.mNote: Repeated B and C beneath slow-moving lines

sections.label: A′ · E minor bursts back
sections.mNote: Soft pedal released; the opening returns fortissimo

sections.label: Coda · Clipped E-minor chords
sections.mNote: A quiet phrase grows into the staccato ending

cues.title: A bass with teeth
cues.text: The left hand is marked ben marcato — strongly marked — beneath the running tune. E minor, fortissimo, Prestissimo: the quiet end of the first movement is a long way away. Even the second theme, in B minor, keeps the restless character of the first.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 16 No. 153, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 101. The relation between the themes is discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass takes over
cues.text: The middle passage grows from the opening bass line. Repeated Bs, then Cs, support notes that move slowly above them. The running quavers eventually stop; the hands answer one another softly, with the soft pedal down.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 102: repeated bass notes and una corda. Gerald Larner identifies the opening bass as the source of the middle section: https://geraldlarner.com/work/beethoven-sonata-in-e-major-op-109.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: All the strings again
cues.text: The opening comes back fortissimo in E minor. Beethoven writes tutte le corde: the pianist releases the soft pedal, allowing the hammers to strike all their strings again. After the whispered exchanges, those first bass octaves have a startling force.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 102–103: una corda and sempre più piano precede the return, marked tutte le corde and ff. Score: https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “A dedication!”
cues.text: In December 1821 Beethoven sends the sonata to Maximiliane Brentano in Frankfurt, daughter of his friends Franz and Antonie Brentano. “A dedication!” he writes. “But not one of those that so many people use and abuse.”
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Maximiliane Brentano, Vienna, 6 December 1821 (autograph, private ownership), printed at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/Opus109/. Her parents: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).

transitions.title: The opening bass comes forward
transitions.from: A · E minor, then B minor
transitions.to: Dev · The bass becomes the tune
transitions.how: After the B-minor second theme, Beethoven develops the opening bass. The piano settles over repeated B, the dominant of E minor, while the right hand stretches into longer notes. The bass then rises to C. The Prestissimo marking stays in force as the hands gradually shed their running quavers.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 102; Gerald Larner’s Op. 109 programme note identifies the opening bass as the middle section’s source. https://geraldlarner.com/work/beethoven-sonata-in-e-major-op-109

transitions.title: Soft pedal, then fortissimo
transitions.from: Dev · The bass becomes the tune
transitions.how: The repeated bass stops. With the soft pedal down, the hands exchange phrases marked sempre più piano, quieter and quieter, and pause under a fermata. A few hushed chords remain before tutte le corde and fortissimo restore the opening E-minor tune above its bass octaves.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 102–103: una corda, sempre più piano, fermata, then the ff return. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

transitions.title: The bass drops, the chords climb
transitions.how: A quiet closing phrase sets the hands moving apart: the bass steps down while chords climb in the right hand. The crescendo ends in three clipped chords, marked forte staccato, with E minor firmly under the fingers.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 104, final system of the Prestissimo. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
